content_record.title: A better body-fat measure undercuts the childhood 'fat rebound' theory
content_record.editorial_body: A more accurate measure shows body fat doesn't rebound in kids; BMI rise may be muscle growth. Study challenges 42-year-old theory of childhood fat rebound. BMI rises around age 6, but body fat doesn't. Increase likely from muscle and lean tissue growth. The modern study uses a more accurate body-fat measure (likely dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry or air-displacement plethysmography) to show that the BMI rebound around age 6 is driven by an increase in fat-free mass (muscle and lean tissue), not fat mass. This directly validates Keys' 1972 caution that BMI is a proxy for weight relative to height, not adiposity. Mechanistically, the rebound coincides with the developmental surge in growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), which promote muscle protein synthesis and skeletal growth, while fat mass remains stable or declines. The historical somatotype framework of Sheldon similarly separated muscularity from fatness, and this finding provides quantitative confirmation that BMI conflates these compartments, leading to a false 'fat rebound' that is actually a 'lean rebound.' This signal is based on A 42-year-old childhood obesity theory may be wrong from ScienceDaily Healthy Aging. Read the original report for full context.
